public_rationale: The New Yorker’s October 3, 2016 report describes a May 2016 meeting where Amodei told Altman and Brockman that people believed OpenAI would release its AI source code publicly [e1]. Altman reportedly replied, “We don’t plan to release all of our source code,” followed by “But let’s please not try to correct that” [e1]. This reported exchange supports the narrow claim that Altman acknowledged the misconception and asked that it remain uncorrected at that opportunity [e1].
limitations: The supplied evidence consists of one reported account; no independent recording, transcript, or meeting minutes are supplied.
The account does not establish who originated the misconception, whether it was corrected later, or what other OpenAI employees knew.

public_payload.normalized_proposition: OpenAI knew it was misleading people into believing it meant open-sourced AI and failed to take an opportunity, at a May 2016 meeting, to correct that belief.
conditions: at the May 2016 meeting described by The New Yorker

statement.excerpt: They knew they were misleading people and failed to take an opportunity to correct.

our_interpretation: The claim concerns the May 2016 meeting described in The New Yorker, not a conditional forecast.
They refers to the OpenAI leaders present, specifically Altman and Brockman.
The plain reading is that leadership learned of a mistaken public belief about releasing source code and chose to leave it uncorrected.
This does not require proving that leadership originally created every instance of the misconception.
criteria.support_condition: The meeting account records that leaders were told of the open-source misconception, acknowledged a different actual intention, and chose not to correct it.
criteria.contradiction_condition: The account shows that leaders corrected the misconception, did not recognize it, or made a materially different statement.
